q: Does pyuria convert asymptomatic bacteriuria into symptomatic UTI?
o: No - pyuria excludes the presence of bacteria in urine
No - asymptomatic bacteriuria can occur with or without pyuria
Yes - pyuria alone establishes symptomatic UTI
Yes - all bacteria in urine indicate symptomatic infection
explanation:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria can occur with or without pyuria when localizing genitourinary signs and symptoms are absent (p1699).

C. Yes - pyuria alone establishes symptomatic UTI: The ASB definition explicitly permits pyuria without localizing symptoms (p1699).
A. No - pyuria excludes the presence of bacteria in urine: Bacteriuria and pyuria can coexist in ASB (p1699).
D. Yes - all bacteria in urine indicate symptomatic infection: Bacteriuria alone does not supply the localizing symptoms needed to distinguish symptomatic infection (p1699).

q: What distinguishes simple cystitis from complicated UTI in this chapter?
o: Simple cystitis is bladder-confined; complicated UTI extends beyond the bladder
Complicated UTI is defined by the absence of all systemic symptoms
Any pyuria makes cystitis complicated, regardless of infection location
Simple cystitis involves renal parenchyma; complicated UTI is bladder-confined
explanation:
Simple cystitis is confined to the bladder, whereas complicated UTI extends beyond it, including renal-parenchymal infection (p1700).

D. Simple cystitis involves renal parenchyma; complicated UTI is bladder-confined: Renal-parenchymal infection is pyelonephritis and is classified as complicated (p1700).
C. Any pyuria makes cystitis complicated, regardless of infection location: Pyuria also accompanies simple cystitis; extension beyond the bladder distinguishes complicated UTI (p1700).
B. Complicated UTI is defined by the absence of all systemic symptoms: Fever, rigors and other systemic signs commonly suggest infection beyond the bladder (p1700).

q: Does a high postvoid residual consistently predict symptomatic UTI?
o: Yes - all ambulatory and nursing-home studies found an association
Yes - a high residual alone establishes symptomatic infection
No - every study excludes postvoid residual as a risk factor
No - prospective studies did not consistently find an association
explanation:
Postvoid-residual studies conflict, with prospective studies failing to find a consistent association with symptomatic UTI (p1702).

A. Yes - all ambulatory and nursing-home studies found an association: The ambulatory and nursing-home prospective studies described did not (p1702).
C. No - every study excludes postvoid residual as a risk factor: An earlier case-control study identified residual urine among recurrent-UTI risk factors (p1702).
B. Yes - a high residual alone establishes symptomatic infection: Residual volume is not a substitute for the clinical symptomatic-UTI definition, and prospective findings conflict (p1700, p1702).

q: What ASB-treatment exception is specified for older adults?
o: Whenever pyuria accompanies asymptomatic bacteriuria
For every asymptomatic older resident of a long-term-care facility
Before endoscopic urologic procedures associated with mucosal trauma
For a change in urine odor alone without localizing symptoms
explanation:
Screening for and treating ASB is recommended before endoscopic urologic procedures associated with mucosal trauma (p1703).

A. Whenever pyuria accompanies asymptomatic bacteriuria: ASB can include pyuria, and treatment is not recommended merely for bacteriuria in asymptomatic older adults (p1699, p1703).
B. For every asymptomatic older resident of a long-term-care facility: The guidance recommends against this except for specified urologic procedures (p1703).
D. For a change in urine odor alone without localizing symptoms: Urine-character change is insufficient to indicate UTI (p1705).

q: Should a urine color or odor change alone establish UTI?
o: Yes - diet and medications cannot alter urine character
No - urine-character change alone is insufficient to indicate UTI
Yes - a change in urine odor establishes infection without symptoms
No - urine-character changes cannot occur with dehydration
explanation:
Urine-character changes alone are insufficient to indicate UTI and can reflect dehydration, diet or medications (p1705).

C. Yes - a change in urine odor establishes infection without symptoms: The text says urine-character change is insufficient (p1705).
D. No - urine-character changes cannot occur with dehydration: Mild dehydration is a stated alternative explanation (p1705).
A. Yes - diet and medications cannot alter urine character: Changes in diet or medications are stated alternative explanations (p1705).

q: Can an older man have simple cystitis?
o: Yes - men can have bladder-confined acute simple cystitis
No - first-line cystitis agents differ completely between men and women
No - male sex alone makes every UTI complicated
Yes - infection extending beyond the bladder remains simple cystitis
explanation:
Men can have acute simple cystitis; assess carefully for signs that infection extends beyond the bladder (p1710).

C. No - male sex alone makes every UTI complicated: The book rejects automatically classifying all male UTI episodes as complicated (p1710).
D. Yes - infection extending beyond the bladder remains simple cystitis: Beyond-bladder infection is complicated UTI (p1700, p1710).
B. No - first-line cystitis agents differ completely between men and women: The book lists the same first-line agents for men and women (p1710).

q: When may a week of antibiotics suffice for an older man with simple cystitis?
o: When the response is delayed beyond the prompt-response interval
Whenever infection extends beyond the bladder, regardless of severity
Whenever fever persists, regardless of response to antibiotics
When the response is prompt, within 72 hours
explanation:
For most older men with acute simple cystitis, seven days is adequate if response is prompt, within 72 hours (p1711).

A. When the response is delayed beyond the prompt-response interval: The seven-day recommendation is conditional on prompt response; delayed response can justify longer treatment (p1710-1711).
C. Whenever fever persists, regardless of response to antibiotics: The text conditions the simple-cystitis recommendation on prompt response, and febrile UTI had different short-term outcomes (p1711).
B. Whenever infection extends beyond the bladder, regardless of severity: Complicated UTI requires management according to severity and is outside this simple-cystitis recommendation (p1711).
